items.title: Returning the first samples from a Martian moon: Inside the science of Japan's bold MMX mission to Mars
items.snippet: Japan's mission to Mars' moons could answer a decades old question dividing the origins of Phobos and Deimos between two conflicting theories, and make history as the first spacecraft to return to Earth from orbit of the Red Planet.

items.title: Computer scientist Margaret Hamilton was a problem-solver for the ages (op-ed)
items.snippet: The world will miss Margaret Hamilton, the pioneering programmer who helped NASA land Apollo astronauts on the moon. But we will always have her example to inspire us.

items.title: 'A uniquely direct route that might cause damage': Scientists uncover link between air pollution and eye diseases like glaucoma
items.snippet: A review of 41 studies found that higher exposure to air pollution was linked to greater odds of glaucoma and cataracts, with PM2.5 pollution showing the clearest association.

items.title: Who's paying whom? The circular money machine behind the AI boom (or bubble)
items.snippet: Imagine a company that sells you equipment, invests money in your business and then rents back what you build with it. It's your supplier, your investor and your customer all at once.

items.title: Ancient Nubian temple faience workshop reveals links between craft production and royal power
items.snippet: Archaeologists have discovered a faience workshop at a major temple complex in the ancient Nubian capital of Napata, showing how the rulers of ancient Kush used specialized craft production to reinforce royal power.

items.title: Early humans in America endured climate chaos—new research
items.snippet: Some 23,000 years ago, during the coldest part of the last ice age, people walked across the muddy margins of an ancient lake in what is now White Sands National Park, New Mexico.

items.title: Earth's oldest evidence of life is written in stone—but it's at risk of disappearing
items.snippet: Today, our planet is teeming with life, but it has not always looked the same. Long before forests reached skyward, animals walked on land and dinosaurs rose and fell, our planet was shaped by a much smaller, more unassuming form of life. And we can still find traces of it today.

items.title: Japan to launch historic round-trip mission to Mars moon
items.snippet: Japanese scientists are readying a mission to Mars' moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region.

items.title: Spatial genomics tool maps long-range DNA interactions while preserving cells' locations within tissues
items.snippet: DNA is not randomly distributed within the nucleus but is packaged with proteins into chromatin, which is precisely folded into complex three-dimensional structures. However, scientists have not fully understood how this complex three-dimensional (3D) organization is regulated or how it changes over time.

items.title: Dozens of orangutans saved from Indonesia blazes as region grapples with haze
items.snippet: Dozens of critically endangered orangutans have been rescued in recent weeks from rampant wildfires burning across Indonesia that have cloaked the region in toxic haze, conservation groups said.

items.title: Climate change affects the quality of one of the world's most important staple foods
items.snippet: Depending on the cultivar, higher concentrations of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the atmosphere can significantly alter the protein composition of wheat. This affects not only baking quality but potentially also the tolerability of wheat products. items.title: New monolithic ion trap opens quantum simulations to more researchers
items.snippet: Some quantum systems are so complex that even the most powerful supercomputers struggle to simulate their behavior. One solution is quantum simulation: building a controllable quantum system in the lab and tuning it to mimic the one researchers want to understand.

items.title: A new way to detect stabilizing properties of optical devices
items.snippet: In optical fibers, chips and other light-guiding devices, minor defects can scatter photons and disrupt their path. A new study demonstrates a way to reveal properties which, in certain systems, help light wave behavior withstand such flaws. The method could help speed up the search for new kinds of electronics and optical technologies, and contribute to more reliable quantum devices.

items.title: BBC visits wildfire front in haze-choked Indonesia
items.snippet: The BBC is in central Kalimantan, where a toxic haze fuelled by wildfires is choking millions of residents.

items.title: Mission set to blast off for Mars to grab a piece of its moon
items.snippet: A spacecraft is set to launch on an ambitious mission to bring 10g of Martian moon dust back to Earth.

items.title: 26 Oct = 25 years since: President George W. Bush signed the Patriot Act into law, significantly expanding the authority of United States law enforcement agencies.
items.snippet: George Walker Bush is an American former politician, businessman, and U.S. Air Force veteran who served as the 43rd president of the United States from 2001 to 2009. A member of the Republican Party, he served as the 46th governor of Texas from 1995 to 2000. He is the eldest son of George H. W. Bush
